text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure your blood sugar or average glucose levels.
snippet_highlighted_words: using specific blood tests that measure your blood sugar or average glucose levels

text_blocks.snippet: According to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association and the Mayo Clinic, type 2 diabetes is confirmed if you meet any of the following thresholds:

list.snippet: A1C Test (Glycated Hemoglobin): 6.5% or higher (measures average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months; no fasting required).
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: 126 mg/dL or higher (taken in the morning after at least an 8-hour fast without food or drink except water).
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): 200 mg/dL or higher (measured 2 hours after drinking a 75-gram glucose solution).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: 200 mg/dL or higher (taken at any time of day, used if you have classic symptoms of high blood sugar like frequent urination or extreme thirst).
Repeat Testing: Except in cases of severe symptoms with a high random glucose reading, doctors typically confirm the result by repeating one of the diagnostic tests on a subsequent day.
Prediabetes Range: If your results fall between an A1C of 5.7%–6.4%, a fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL, or an OGTT of 140–199 mg/dL, it indicates prediabetes.

Screening Recommendations: Routine screening is recommended for adults starting at age 35, or earlier if you have risk factors such as overweight or obesity, a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure, or a history of gestational diabetes.
